clue.text: Current President assumed he had succeeded (9)

indicators.note: To assume something is to take it on and absorb it, so the word doing the assuming closes over the letter named beside it.

blocks.note: the surname of the sitting US president, five letters straight off the front page
I is the physics symbol for electric current and the crossword's standard way of clueing it
he had contracts to he'd, and the grid has no room for an apostrophe

explanation.surface: A head of state taking it as read that a man had already got where he wanted to be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current President' reads as one phrase naming whoever is in office now, which is the whole of the misdirection: the two words belong to different pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: succeeded → TRIUMPHED: both are past-tense verbs for coming out on top, though 'succeeded' covers merely managing it where the answer claims an outright win.

clue.text: Corporation covering it in a molten metal (8)

indicators.note: A cover goes over a thing on every side, so the word doing the covering wraps right round what comes next.
Metal gone molten has lost its shape completely, and letters in that state will not hold the order they were handed over in.

blocks.note: a corporation is an old word for a paunch, the belly a well-fed alderman carries in front of him
five small words' worth of letters, run together and melted into a new order

explanation.surface: A firm quietly hiding something small by dropping it into a bath of molten metal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corporation' is planted to look like a company and it is the Victorian sense, a man's belly — the same joke Dickens would have made.
explanation.definitionFit: metal → TITANIUM: definition by example, since titanium is one metal among dozens and the plain noun is standing in for the particular element.

clue.text: Find keen lads in prime locations getting tattooed (5)

indicators.note: The locations wanted are the prime-numbered ones: number the letters straight through and keep those standing at 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11.

blocks.note: twelve letters run together, with the ones at prime positions picked off in order

explanation.surface: Advice on where to look for the keenest lads, all of them covered in tattoos.
explanation.walkthrough: Prime numbers are a rare device and the giveaway is that 'prime locations' is estate-agent talk for the best spots, doing surface duty at the same time.
explanation.definitionFit: tattooed → INKED: ink is what a tattooist works in, so the past participle has become the ordinary word for having had the work done.

clue.text: Bill might arrive in this capital before eleven, worried about work (6,8)

indicators.note: What stands before something else is written first, so the capital's six letters open the answer and the rest follows.
To worry a thing is to shake it about the way a dog worries a rag, and letters shaken like that come back out of order.

blocks.note: the capital of the Philippines
the number spelled out in full, handing over its six letters to be shuffled
OP is a work — opus — the label printed on every piece of classical music

explanation.surface: Somebody fretting over a bill that might reach them in a far-off capital before eleven o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital before eleven' reads as an appointment in a city, and 'about' is a plain joining word here rather than an instruction to go round anything.
explanation.definitionFit: Bill might arrive in this → MANILA ENVELOPE: the buff office envelope, named for the Manila hemp it was first made from, is what an invoice comes in.

clue.text: Means to cut journalist on Maxim (7)

indicators.note: This entry runs down the grid, so a piece sitting on another is the one written above it and takes the front of the answer.

blocks.note: a hack is a jobbing reporter, and it is not a compliment
a saw is an old proverb — Shakespeare's 'wise saws and modern instances' — and the capital M is the magazine on the surface

explanation.surface: A way of cutting down to size a journalist who writes for a lads' magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics are the trap: they make Maxim a title, and the word wanted is the ordinary noun for a pithy old saying.
explanation.definitionFit: Means to cut → HACKSAW: the phrase names an instrument, and a hacksaw is the fine-toothed blade kept for cutting through metal and pipe.

clue.text: Dundee’s comic strips (7)

indicators.note: Comic is doing service as 'funny' in the sense of odd, and letters called odd have stopped standing in their proper order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters, the apostrophe ignored as punctuation always is

explanation.surface: The comic strips that come out of Dundee, home of the Beano and the Dandy.
explanation.walkthrough: DC Thomson has published the Beano and the Dandy from Dundee for a century, so 'Dundee's comic strips' reads as one solid phrase — and only 'strips' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: strips → DENUDES: third-person verbs both, for taking the covering off something, whether that is a person, a hillside or a papered wall.

clue.text: Soot – small amount oddly disappears (4)

indicators.note: The odd ones are the letters going missing, so strike out the first, third and fifth and read off whatever survives.

blocks.note: S is the size in a shirt collar and the standard abbreviation for small
a, o and n stand at positions one, three and five; take them out and three letters remain

explanation.surface: Soot, with a tiny quantity of it going missing here and there.
explanation.walkthrough: A smut is a single flake of soot, the sort that settles on washing near a chimney; the word's other sense, dirty talk, is what 15 down leans on.
explanation.definitionFit: Soot → SMUT: a smut is a flake of soot or the black mark it leaves, so the two nouns name the same speck of chimney dirt.

clue.text: Graduate, 22 aimed to work in TV, radio etc (4,5)

indicators.note: Working a thing means kneading it about, the way a baker works dough, and letters worked over like that end up in a new arrangement.

blocks.note: Master of Arts, the letters a graduate puts after their name
22 across is a steamship, and SS is the pair of letters painted before such a vessel's name
five letters handed over to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A graduate with ambitions to land a job in broadcasting.
explanation.walkthrough: The 22 sends you across the grid: solve that entry first and it hands back two letters, which is why a cross-reference is worth doing early.
explanation.definitionFit: TV, radio etc → MASS MEDIA: the plural noun covers the channels that reach a whole population at once, of which broadcasting is the everyday example.

clue.text: Thus far, ultimately not, old fruit (2,4)

indicators.note: What happens ultimately happens last, so only the final letter of the word beside it is being offered.

blocks.note: the last letter of not
O is the standard abbreviation for old
the sticky brown fruit of the palm

explanation.surface: Someone reporting that the answer is still no, and addressing a friend as 'old fruit'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old fruit' is dated British chumminess, roughly 'old chap', and the surface leans on it hard while the wordplay quietly splits the phrase in two.
explanation.definitionFit: Thus far → TO DATE: both adverbial phrases mean up to the present moment, and either can end a sentence about how much has happened so far.

clue.text: Fix up 8 panels illustrating hero-worship (3,2,1,8)

indicators.note: Fixing something means pulling it apart and putting the parts back another way, which is exactly what happens to these fourteen letters.

blocks.note: 8 down is TO DATE, so this reads as up-to-date panels — fourteen letters in all

explanation.surface: An instruction to repair some modern display boards showing somebody being idolised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fix up' wants to be read as one phrasal verb, and that is what buries the cross-reference: the 'up' belongs with the 8, not with the fixing.
explanation.definitionFit: hero-worship → PUT ON A PEDESTAL: to hero-worship someone is to set them above ordinary judgement, which is what the idiom's raised plinth pictures.

clue.text: Representation of crypto Musk finally invested in X (5)

indicators.note: Finally asks for the ends of the words in front of it, so each one gives up its closing letter and nothing else.
Money invested in something is put inside it, and these letters go bodily into the middle of the piece that follows.

blocks.note: X is the Roman numeral for ten, spelled out in letters here
the closing letters of crypto and of Musk, taken in that order

explanation.surface: Elon Musk sinking the last of his money into a cryptocurrency on his own platform.
explanation.walkthrough: X does three jobs on the surface — Musk's platform, the unknown quantity, the kiss — and the wordplay wants none of them, only the Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Representation → TOKEN: a token stands in for something else, a bus fare or a promise, which is what a representation does; the crypto sense is the newest branch.

clue.text: Stunned prisoner swore (9)

blocks.note: a con is a convict, the crossword's usual prisoner
to cuss is to swear, so its past tense is six letters long

explanation.surface: A prisoner still reeling from a knock on the head, letting fly with language.
explanation.walkthrough: CON for prisoner is the most-worked abbreviation in the British cryptic, and 'cuss' is the American softening of 'curse' that setters here borrow freely.
explanation.definitionFit: Stunned → CONCUSSED: both past participles describe somebody knocked senseless by a blow, concussed being the medical version of the same daze.

clue.text: Nintendo console installing game after turning knobs (7)

indicators.note: Installing a thing means fitting it inside whatever will hold it, so this piece drops into the middle of the one before.
The game is turned round before it goes in, so its letters are written out from the back end forwards.

blocks.note: the Nintendo Entertainment System, the 1980s machine everybody called by its initials
ludo, the counters-and-dice race game, written backwards

explanation.surface: A Nintendo machine with a game slotted into it and its control knobs given a twist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nintendo console' looks like one indivisible phrase naming a box under the telly, and what the clue wants is the machine's own initials.
explanation.definitionFit: knobs → NODULES: both plural nouns for small rounded lumps standing up from a surface, nodules being the word a doctor or a geologist reaches for.

clue.text: One looked down on party leader abandoning make-up (7)

indicators.note: A word's leader is the letter at its head, and here that letter is the one walking out, so what remains begins one letter in.

blocks.note: a do is a party — 'a bit of a do' — and it is the crossword's standard one
the make-up of a thing is its FORMAT, which here gives up its opening F

explanation.surface: Contempt for a party leader who has stopped bothering with make-up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party leader' reads as one phrase naming a politician, and the two words belong to different pieces of wordplay: the party is the knees-up.
explanation.definitionFit: One looked down on → DOORMAT: it lies at the threshold and is literally looked down on, and the same word names a person everybody walks over.

clue.text: Slogan – one used by Kanye and GAP before silly flawed deal’s conclusion (6,2,5,7,2,4)

annotation.answer: UNITED WE STAND DIVIDED WE FALL

indicators.note: What comes before something else is written ahead of it, so the gap's letters land in front of the shuffled ones.
Something silly has no sense left in the way it is arranged, and letters called silly will not be standing in the order they arrived in.
A word's conclusion is where it stops, so only the last letter of the one beside it is being handed over.

blocks.note: an adjective here: a party or a country that acts as one has joined into a single body
the surname Kanye goes by
lifted straight out of the clue, letter for letter
a gap between two camps is what a newspaper calls a rift, and the capitals are the shop on the surface
six letters handed over to be shaken up
the letter the word deal stops on

explanation.surface: Kanye West's clothing tie-up with Gap, and the daft, botched way that deal came to an end.
explanation.walkthrough: The two entries tell the story in order: the first is the collaboration, the second the collapse. Kanye supplies his surname, not his music.
explanation.definitionFit: Slogan → UNITED WE STAND, DIVIDED WE FALL: the proverb has been a rallying motto since the American Revolution and is the state motto of Kentucky.

clue.text: Good taste, home before 6? (9)

indicators.note: Whatever goes before goes first, so the two letters meaning at home are written ahead of the longer piece.

blocks.note: somebody at home is in, the way a caller finds them
not taste in food or furniture but in the moral sense, the propriety that keeps people from giving offence

explanation.surface: Good manners, and getting back to the house before six o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: The 6 is a cross-reference and not a time: solve 6 across and you are holding the definition, which is what the question mark is apologising for.
explanation.definitionFit: 6 → INDECENCY: 6 across is SMUT, and indecency is the abstract noun for the same thing, material that offends against public decency.

clue.text: State of Mar-a-Lago after detailing walls of lavatory in a rococo style (8)

indicators.note: De-tailing a word is docking its tail, so the state named beside it arrives with its final letter cut off.
The walls of a building are its outermost surfaces, so take the first and last letters of the word that follows and nothing between.

blocks.note: Mar-a-Lago is Trump's Palm Beach club, so the state is Florida, arriving here one letter short
the two outermost letters of lavatory, one from each end

explanation.surface: The state a Florida resort is in once it has been stripped back and its lavatory done out in gilt curlicues.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' reads as condition and means the US state, and 'detailing' reads as car valeting when it is de-tailing, docking a final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: in a rococo style → FLORIDLY: the adverb means ornately, in a manner loaded with flourish, which is exactly how rococo decoration is applied.

clue.text: See 14
Worry ad-libs occasionally dry up (7)

indicators.note: Something done occasionally happens every so often rather than every time, so only every second letter of the word beside it is picked up.
This entry is written from the top downwards, so a piece told to go up is read from its bottom end back to its top.

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of the word, the hyphen counting for nothing
brut is the dry style printed on a champagne label, and here it is climbing the grid

explanation.surface: An improviser's off-the-cuff lines drying up every now and again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dry up' is one phrase on the surface, the thing that happens to a performer who loses their lines, and the wordplay takes the two words apart.
explanation.definitionFit: Worry → DISTURB: as verbs both mean to unsettle somebody's peace of mind, and 'do not disturb' asks the same thing as 'do not trouble'.

clue.text: Object in stock, we hear (7)

indicators.note: What we hear is the sound and not the spelling, so the answer is written the way a different word is said aloud.

blocks.note: stock in the sense of ancestry — 'of good stock' — is descent, and said aloud it comes out spelled another way

explanation.surface: An objection raised about goods sitting in the storeroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In stock' wants to be one phrase about a warehouse; the wordplay needs 'stock' alone, and in the breeding sense rather than the inventory one.
explanation.definitionFit: Object → DISSENT: both verbs mean registering that you do not agree, with dissent carrying the formal note of a minority voting the other way.

clue.text: Question of motive consumes one writing fantasy (6)

indicators.note: Whatever a word consumes it swallows whole, so the pieces named after it end up held inside it.

blocks.note: the question you ask when what you want is a motive
the Roman numeral for one, the crossword's usual way of writing it
MS is a manuscript, a piece of writing before anyone sets it in type

explanation.surface: A detective's question about motive swallowing up a novelist of fantasy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One writing' reads as a person who writes, which is the trap — it is two separate scraps, a numeral and an abbreviation, laid end to end.
explanation.definitionFit: fantasy → WHIMSY: whimsy is playful fancy, the light end of fantasy, invention followed for its own oddity rather than a whole imagined world.

clue.text: Spots French disappearing behind hospital barracks (7)

indicators.note: French is FR in wordplay, and disappearing says those two letters are the ones taken out of the word beside it.
This entry runs left to right, so a piece placed behind another comes after it and fills the tail of the answer.

blocks.note: H is the standard abbreviation, the letter on the road sign
the spots are FRECKLES, and the two letters standing for French come away from the front

explanation.surface: Spots on a French visitor fading from view behind the barracks by the hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barracks' is placed to read as army buildings next to the hospital, and it is a verb: to barrack is British and Australian for jeering at a player or speaker.
explanation.definitionFit: barracks → HECKLES: to barrack somebody is to shout them down from the crowd, and both verbs are the third-person singular of that same nuisance.

clue.text: Ship’s pilot eats before noon (7)

indicators.note: What a word eats it takes inside itself, so the letters named next sit in the middle of it rather than alongside.

blocks.note: to pilot a boat is to steer it — the verb, not the man on the bridge
the hours before noon are the am ones on a clock face

explanation.surface: A ship's pilot having a bite to eat before midday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ship's pilot' reads as one job title and then splits: 'Ship' is the definition on its own, and the apostrophe-s does the work of an equals sign.
explanation.definitionFit: Ship → STEAMER: definition by example — a steamer is one kind of ship, the steam-driven sort, so the general noun stands for the particular.

clue.text: Case of Maserati on motorway going over 100, makes Mirror (5)

indicators.note: A case is what encloses a thing, so what is wanted is the outside letters of the word and not its contents.
This entry runs down the grid, so a piece sitting on another is written above it.
Going over something is passing above it, so whatever this piece goes over is written underneath it.

blocks.note: the first and last letters of Maserati
the M1 is Britain's first motorway, and in a grid of capitals its numeral is read as a letter I
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

explanation.surface: A Maserati flying up the motorway past a hundred, caught in the rear-view mirror.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics make Mirror the newspaper, which is the whole misdirection — it is the plain verb. Reading the M1's digit as a capital I is the step to spot.
explanation.definitionFit: Mirror → MIMIC: both are verbs for copying somebody's movements straight back at them, one from the glass and one from the impressionist.

clue.text: The change made on vacation without delay … (9)

indicators.note: A word sent on vacation has been emptied of its occupants, so the middle letters go and only the two ends stay behind.

blocks.note: the outside letters of made, with the middle two cleared out
doing a thing without delay is doing it with no pause

explanation.surface: Alterations carried out while the family is away on holiday, and done straight away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The change' is the euphemism a doctor's waiting room would use, and the trailing dots hand the word 'change' straight on to 25 across, where it does a different job.
explanation.definitionFit: The change → MENOPAUSE: 'the change', or 'the change of life', is the long-standing British euphemism for it, so the two nouns name one event.

clue.text: … change made on time – now under control (5)

indicators.note: Letters told to change do not keep the arrangement they came in, and this is the same word 24 across used as its definition.

blocks.note: the four letters of made plus T, the standard abbreviation for time — five to rearrange

explanation.surface: An alteration delivered on schedule, with everything now running smoothly.
explanation.walkthrough: The dots carry 'change' over from 24 across, where it was the definition; here the very same word is the instruction to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: now under control → TAMED: a tamed animal, river or temper has been brought to heel, and the past participle carries the 'now' of a finished change.

clue.text: Type of dieting you endlessly repeated (2-2)

definitions.note: YO-YO is a noun and 'Type of dieting' asks for the modifier in 'yo-yo dieting'; setters allow this because the toy's name is what supplies the sense.

indicators.note: A word taken endlessly has had its end removed, so the final letter of the one beside it is dropped before anything else happens.

blocks.note: the word you with its last letter taken off
the same two letters come round a second time

explanation.surface: The kind of dieting somebody keeps going back to, over and over again.
explanation.walkthrough: Yo-yo dieting is weight lost and regained in cycles, named for the toy that comes straight back up the string the moment you drop it.
explanation.definitionFit: Type of dieting → YO-YO: the word attaches to dieting to name the up-and-down pattern, losing the same weight and putting it back on repeatedly.

clue.text: Book new cattery to accommodate Lambert and Geronimo? (6-3)

indicators.note: Something made new has been put together again out of the same parts, and letters rebuilt that way come out in a different order.
To accommodate a guest is to find room for them inside, so the letter named next is fitted into the middle of what precedes it.

blocks.note: B is the standard abbreviation for book
seven letters rebuilt into a shell with a gap left in the middle of it
the lambert is the old unit of brightness, and its symbol is a single L

explanation.surface: Reserving space in a newly built cattery for two arrivals called Lambert and Geronimo.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a definition by example. Only one of the two names defines anything — the other is a unit of measurement dressed up as a pet.
explanation.definitionFit: Geronimo → BATTLE-CRY: 'Geronimo!' is what American paratroopers yelled leaving the aircraft, so the Apache leader's name became one particular battle-cry.
